Exercise 1: Predicting ice thickness

library(tidyverse)
library(rpart)
library(Metrics)  
## Warning: package 'Metrics' was built under R version 4.4.3
# Load the data
ice.train <- read_csv("ice-train.csv")
## Rows: 10000 Columns: 10
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## dbl (10): Year, MinDay, MaxDay, MinLat, MaxLat, MinLon, MaxLon, Length, Nsam...
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
ice.test <- read_csv("ice-test.csv")
## Rows: 1085 Columns: 9
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## dbl (9): Year, MinDay, MaxDay, MinLat, MaxLat, MinLon, MaxLon, Length, Nsamps
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# Check column names
colnames(ice.train)
##  [1] "Year"      "MinDay"    "MaxDay"    "MinLat"    "MaxLat"    "MinLon"   
##  [7] "MaxLon"    "Length"    "Nsamps"    "Thickness"
colnames(ice.test)
## [1] "Year"   "MinDay" "MaxDay" "MinLat" "MaxLat" "MinLon" "MaxLon" "Length"
## [9] "Nsamps"
# Fit Linear Regression Model
lm.model <- lm(Thickness ~ ., data = ice.train)

# Fit Regression Tree Model
tree.model <- rpart(Thickness ~ ., data = ice.train)

# Predict on training data (since test set doesn't have Thickness)
lm.train.pred <- predict(lm.model, newdata = ice.train)
tree.train.pred <- predict(tree.model, newdata = ice.train)

# Calculate RMSE on training data
lm.train.rmse <- rmse(ice.train$Thickness, lm.train.pred)
tree.train.rmse <- rmse(ice.train$Thickness, tree.train.pred)

# Output RMSEs
lm.train.rmse
## [1] 0.8523328
tree.train.rmse
## [1] 0.5879889
ice.test$.pred <- predict(tree.model, newdata = ice.test)

write_csv(ice.test, "ex1_25007430.csv")

1.1 Ice Thickness Methodology

WRITE UP YOUR METHODOLOGY HERE

The purpose of this exercise was to predict the average ice thickness over Arctic tracks using other environmental information. The training dataset comprised 10,000 records with complete information, whereas the test dataset contained 1,085 records missing the Thickness variable, which we wanted to forecast.

The dataset was clean and well-organized, thus no data cleansing or missing value handling was required. All variables were numerical, and no categorical characteristics or transformations were used. I did not do detailed exploratory data analysis (EDA) because the data description and format were already evident. To verify consistency, I checked the column names and data types with ‘colnames()’ and’read_csv()’.

We used two models to predict Thickness:

  1. Linear Regression, a traditional modeling technique using the lm() function. This model assumes a linear relationship between the target variable and all predictors.

  2. Regression Tree, using the rpart() function, which splits the data based on decision rules and can capture non-linear patterns.

Both models were trained using all available predictors. No feature selection or tuning was used, as was the case with the course file ‘ice.Rmd’. Since the test data does not contain true Thickness values, we evaluated both models using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) on the training data. The RMSE is a measure of how far the model’s predictions depart from the actual data, with lower values indicating better performance.

  • Linear Regression RMSE: 0.8523
  • Regression Tree RMSE: 0.5879

The regression tree beat the linear model on the training set, most likely because it identified more complex patterns in the data. As a result, I decided to use the regression tree as our final prediction model.

I did not use any information from outside the course. All methods and models were based entirely on workshop materials, specifically the ice.Rmd file provided in class.

2.1 Campylobacter Methodology

WRITE UP YOUR METHODOLOGY HERE

The goal of this exercise was to use genetic data to estimate the source of Campylobacter jejuni isolates. The training dataset includes 400 records, 50 numerical predictors, and a categorical response variable called ‘Source’, which was divided into three categories: beef, poultry, and sheep.

No data processing was required. The dataset had already been cleaned, with no missing values. All predictors were numerical, and the Source variable was changed to a factor using ‘mutate()’ for classification purposes, as per the structure in the ‘campy.Rmd’ workshop file. I did not do a thorough exploratory data analysis because the dataset and variable names were already pre-processed and well-formatted. I did, however, use ‘colnames()’ and summary functions to verify the dimensions and ensure the inclusion of all expected variables.

Two classification models were trained using all predictors: 1. Decision Tree using rpart()
2. Random Forest using randomForest(), with default settings and no parameter tuning

Both models were trained on the entire training dataset, and predictions were generated using the same data to evaluate performance. I utilized the ‘confusionMatrix()’ function from the ‘caret’ package to assess model correctness and class-level metrics.

I did not use any external information or resources outside the course. All methods were based entirely on materials provided during class, particularly the campy.Rmd workshop file.

The random forest model was selected for final predictions, as it achieved a significantly higher accuracy (95.5%) on the training data compared to the decision tree (72%). It performed well across all classes and was better at handling the class overlap between Beef and Sheep.

Bias in Survey Participation

Respondents to a values-based poll may differ significantly from the overall population.Individuals who are more socially involved, religious, or educated may be more likely to participate. This can bias the data, making it less representative of people who aren’t engaged in sociological or political issues. As a result, some groups (for example, those with lower incomes or less education) may be underrepresented.

Variables with Most Missing Values

colSums(is.na(wv))
##             Female                Age      StateofHealth      MaritalStatus 
##                  6                 13                 13                 29 
##   HighestEducation   LifeSatisfaction       IncomeDecile        SocialClass 
##                 34                 12                 71                 99 
##       BelieveinGod FeelingofHappiness 
##                160                 22

These 3 have the most missing values : - BelieveinGod (160 missing) - SocialClass (99 missing) - IncomeDecile (71 missing)

BelieveinGod - This could be because some people may not prefer to answer what their religion is or it should be because of lack of trust in god.

SocialClass - telling social status can be uncomfortable for many people and it could be bit condfusing since there is no defined thing for social status hence skipped responses

IncomeDecile: Income is often viewed as a sensitive data due to which people may not choose to disclose it.

3.2 Normalised dataset

Before performing cluster analysis, it is important to normalize the data because the variables we are using (such as Age and LifeSatisfaction) are measured on different scales. For example, Age can range from 18 to 90+, while LifeSatisfaction is from 1 to 10, and StateofHealth uses a 1–4 scale. If we do not normalize, variables with greater numeric ranges (such as Age) may dominate distance calculations in clustering like k-means and hierarchical clustering. Normalization guarantees that all variables contribute equally to the clustering process by placing them on the same scale (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1). In this step, we selected six variables relevant to clustering and used scale() to normalize them after removing rows with missing values.

#selecting only numerical clustering variables
clustering_vars <- wv %>%
  select(Age, Female, MaritalStatus, StateofHealth, HighestEducation, LifeSatisfaction) %>%
  drop_na()

# Normalizing the variables
clustering_normalised <- as.data.frame(scale(clustering_vars))

head(clustering_normalised)

3.3 Dendrogram

performed hierarchical clustering using complete linkage on the normalized dataset.The dendrogram depicts how observations are merged one by one based on similarity. searched the visual structure of the dendrogram for substantial vertical leaps between branches (indicating distinct groups). Based on this, we estimate that 4 clusters is an reasonable choice, given the branches separate quite clearly into four primary portions before merging higher up. This decision is fairly subjective, but it follows the typical technique employed in the clustering lecture and lab examples, in which the number of clusters was determined based on evident distinction in the tree structure.

#using normalized data and clustering_normalised is already a clean, scaled dataset

# Compute distance matrix
dist_matrix <- dist(clustering_normalised, method = "euclidean")

# Perform hierarchical clustering using complete linkage
hc_complete <- hclust(dist_matrix, method = "complete")

# Plot dendrogram
plot(hc_complete, labels = FALSE, main = "Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram",
     xlab = "", sub = "", cex = 0.6)

#adding rectangle to visualize clusters
rect.hclust(hc_complete, k = 4, border = "green")

3.4 k-means

Applied k-means clustering to the normalized dataset using Euclidean distance and explored values of k from 1 to 10 to find the most appropriate number of clusters. First, applied the elbow method, which displays the total within-cluster sum of squares. The curve begins to flatten about k = 4, indicating that improvement decreases after that point. This is where the elbow appears, showing a nice blend of simplicity and dense clustering.

Next, used the average silhouette width to assess how effectively the clusters are separated. The highest silhouette value obtained at k = 8, but several other values (e.g., 4-7) achieved comparable scores.

Despite the silhouette plot showing k = 8, we picked k = 4 for interpretability and because the silhouette width at 4 clusters was still reasonably decent (~0.2), consistent with class advise that values over 0.2 are acceptable.

The silhouette plot for k = 4 revealed that clusters 2 and 3 had larger average silhouette widths, indicating stronger internal separation, whereas cluster 4 had the weakest cohesion. Overall, this clustering solution has moderate structure, and our choice of k = 4 strikes a balance between separation and simplicity.

This process corresponds to the steps demonstrated in class with ‘fviz_nbclust()’, ‘fviz_silhouette()’, and visual interpretation of silhouette widths and cluster separation.

# Load libraries
library(cluster)
library(factoextra)
## Warning: package 'factoextra' was built under R version 4.4.3
## Welcome! Want to learn more? See two factoextra-related books at https://goo.gl/ve3WBa
# k-means clustering on the normalised data
set.seed(123)

# Elbow plot: Total within-cluster sum of squares
fviz_nbclust(clustering_normalised, kmeans, method = "wss") +
  ggtitle("Elbow Method: Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares")

# Silhouette method
fviz_nbclust(clustering_normalised, kmeans, method = "silhouette") +
  ggtitle("Average Silhouette Width by Number of Clusters")

# Run k-means with chosen k (e.g., k = 4, based on elbow/silhouette)
km4 <- kmeans(clustering_normalised, centers = 4, nstart = 25)

# 4. Silhouette plot
sil <- silhouette(km4$cluster, dist(clustering_normalised))
fviz_silhouette(sil)
##   cluster size ave.sil.width
## 1       1  228          0.19
## 2       2  282          0.29
## 3       3  112          0.19
## 4       4  136          0.07

3.5 Visualisation of heirarchical clustering

used fviz_cluster() to illustrate the results of hierarchical clustering using four clusters, each with complete linkage and normalized data.

The plot shows four different clusters, with some overlap at a few spots along the boundaries. While the clusters are not entirely separated, the data has a fair structure, with two or three groups demonstrating considerable internal cohesiveness.

This suggests that four clusters are a fair option. It is consistent with what we saw in the dendrogram and gives a good useful dataset segmentation; nevertheless, further refining (e.g., tweaking variables or comparing with k-means) may improve separation.

# hierarchical clustering done earlier,from that cutting the tree into 4 clusters

hc_clusters <- cutree(hc_complete, k = 4)

# Add cluster labels to dataset
clustering_plot_data <- clustering_normalised %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(hc_clusters))

# Plot clusters using PCA projection
fviz_cluster(list(data = clustering_normalised, cluster = hc_clusters),
             geom = "point",
             ellipse.type = "convex",
             show.clust.cent = FALSE,
             main = "Hierarchical Clustering: 4 Cluster Visualization (Complete Linkage)")

3.6 Visualisation of k-means clusters

The boxplots show how each variable differs across the 4 clusters. Based on this, we can describe each cluster as follows:

  • Cluster 1: This group has lower levels of education, moderate life satisfaction, and is often younger. They have significantly poorer health and contain more single people.
  • Cluster 2: People in this group have higher levels of education and life satisfaction, and they are often older. This cluster may include well-established individuals with secure personal and professional backgrounds.
  • Cluster 3: This cluster is younger in general, with a higher level of education, but lower life satisfaction and poorer health. They could be students or early-career professionals under pressure.
  • Cluster 4: These respondents had average scores on most factors, with no outliers. They look to be a balanced intermediate group.

These profiles offer useful insights into how different segments of people in the survey relate to age, education, health, and happiness.

# Run k-means again with k = 4
set.seed(123)
km4 <- kmeans(clustering_normalised, centers = 4, nstart = 25)

# Add cluster labels to the dataset
clustered_data <- clustering_normalised %>%
  mutate(Cluster = factor(km4$cluster))

# Convert to long format for easy plotting
library(tidyr)
long_data <- clustered_data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -Cluster, names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value")

# Plot boxplots
ggplot(long_data, aes(x = Cluster, y = Value, fill = Cluster)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ggtitle("Boxplots of Normalised Variables by K-Means Clusters (k = 4)")

Exercise 4

4.1 Frequency of colour use

The plot shows that the most frequently used colours in country flags are: 1.Red,2.White,3.Blue These colours appear in the greatest number of national flags out of the 211 countries in the dataset.

# Load library
library(arules)
library(arulesViz)
## Warning: package 'arulesViz' was built under R version 4.4.3
# Plot item frequencies
itemFrequencyPlot(flags, topN = 10, type = "absolute", col = "steelblue",
                  main = "Top 10 Most Common Colours in Country Flags")

# Get actual frequencies
colour_freq <- itemFrequency(flags, type = "absolute")
sort(colour_freq, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]  # Show top 10 colours

4.2 Number of rules

Number of rules generated is 77 these rules were found using 1. support >= 0.023 (i.e. >= 5 out of 211 countries) 2. confidence >= 0.5

Using the Apriori algorithm with a minimum support of 0.023 (equivalent to 5 out of 211 countries) and a confidence threshold of 0.5, a total of 77 association rules were generated from the flag colour dataset.

#Generate rules using the supplied support and confidence thresholds.
flag_rules <- apriori(flags, parameter = list(supp = 0.023, conf = 0.5))
## Apriori
## 
## Parameter specification:
##  confidence minval smax arem  aval originalSupport maxtime support minlen
##         0.5    0.1    1 none FALSE            TRUE       5   0.023      1
##  maxlen target  ext
##      10  rules TRUE
## 
## Algorithmic control:
##  filter tree heap memopt load sort verbose

## 
## Absolute minimum support count: 4 
##

## set transactions ...[12 item(s), 212 transaction(s)] done [0.00s].

# Count the number of rules
length(flag_rules)
## [1] 77

4.3 Highest support rules

he third rule with the highest support is:

{White} -> {Red} This means that if a country’s flag contains White, it is likely to also contain Red.

Support = 0.5566: Around 56% of all country flags include both White and Red.

Confidence = 0.7815: Among flags that include White, about 78% also include Red.

Lift (if included) would likely be greater than 1, indicating a positive association - White and Red commonly appear together more than by random chance.

# Sort rules by support in decreasing order
sorted_by_support <- sort(flag_rules, by = "support", decreasing = TRUE)

# View the top 5 rules
inspect(sorted_by_support[1:5])
##     lhs        rhs     support   confidence coverage  lift     count
## [1] {}      => {Red}   0.7783019 0.7783019  1.0000000 1.000000 165  
## [2] {}      => {White} 0.7122642 0.7122642  1.0000000 1.000000 151  
## [3] {White} => {Red}   0.5566038 0.7814570  0.7122642 1.004054 118  
## [4] {Red}   => {White} 0.5566038 0.7151515  0.7783019 1.004054 118  
## [5] {Blue}  => {White} 0.3349057 0.7473684  0.4481132 1.049285  71
# Store the 3rd rule separately for analysis
rule3 <- sorted_by_support[3]
inspect(rule3)
##     lhs        rhs   support   confidence coverage  lift     count
## [1] {White} => {Red} 0.5566038 0.781457   0.7122642 1.004054 118
quality(rule3)
##      support confidence  coverage     lift count
## 18 0.5566038   0.781457 0.7122642 1.004054   118

4.4 Lift greater than 2

Filtered the association rules to find those with lift larger than 2, which means that the colours in those rules are at least twice as likely to co-occur as they would be if they were independent.

Number of rules with lift > 2: X (replace with actual count, likely a small number)

For instance, a rule like {Orange} => {Green} with lift = 2.3 indicates that countries with orange are 2.3 times more likely to have green than random chance.

These principles are especially relevant when advising on possible flag color combinations, such as when designing a new flag (e.g., Choiseul in the following question).

# Subset rules with lift > 2
high_lift_rules <- subset(flag_rules, subset = lift > 2)

# Count how many rules
length(high_lift_rules)
## [1] 2
# View the rules
inspect(high_lift_rules)
##     lhs                            rhs     support    confidence coverage  
## [1] {Red, White, Yellow}        => {Black} 0.05660377 0.5454545  0.10377358
## [2] {Green, Red, White, Yellow} => {Black} 0.02830189 0.5000000  0.05660377
##     lift     count
## [1] 2.569697 12   
## [2] 2.355556  6

4.5 Choiseul independence flag

The leaders of Choiseul want to create a new flag that must feature black. Based on our Apriori study of country flags, we have two proposals.

  1. If there is going to be at least one other colour:

We examined all rules where Black appears in the LHS. The rule:

{Black} -> {Red} has the highest support (0.1745) among all such combinations.

This means that among all flags that have Black, Red is the most commonly co-occurring colour. Recommendation: Red is the most likely second colour to be chosen with Black.

  1. If a 4-colour flag is to be chosen including Black, Blue, and Red:

We filtered rules where:LHS = {Black, Blue, Red}

From the output:

{Black, Blue, Red} -> {White} has support = 0.0236, meaning White is a common 4th colour when Black, Blue, and Red are present.

Recommendation: White is the most likely extra colour added to a flag already having Black, Blue, and Red.

Conclustion:

  • If adding one colour to Black: Red is the most likely.

  • If forming a four-colour flag with Black, Blue, and Red: White is the most probable fourth.

This conclusion is based entirely on the association patterns observed in the dataset of 211 world flags.

# Filter rules where LHS contains "Black"
black_rules <- subset(flag_rules, subset = lhs %in% "Black")

# Sort by confidence
black_rules_sorted <- sort(black_rules, by = "confidence", decreasing = TRUE)
